An experiment gets written down many times, once per audience:

| Who | What they get |
|---|---|
| The ethics board | a protocol document |
| The public record | a preregistration |
| The participant, or the model | an experiment script |
| The analyst | a notebook |
| The reader | a Methods section and a figure |
| The replicator | whatever survived |

Nothing checks these against each other, so they drift. By the end, no document describes the experiment you ran.

Studyflow replaces them with one file: a diagram you can read, edit, and run.

## Computation and coordination

Code that runs an experiment does two jobs [^gelernter]. It **computes**: presents a stimulus, fits a model, builds a prompt. It **coordinates**: decides what comes next, who joins which group, which file a step reads.

Languages handle computation well. Coordination ends up scattered through the same code, where no one sees it whole and nothing checks it against the protocol.

Studyflow is a coordination notation: it takes the second job out of the code and into a diagram, built on BPMN 2.0 [^bpmn] rather than a new standard.

[^gelernter]: Gelernter, D., & Carriero, N. (1992). Coordination languages and their significance. *Communications of the ACM*, 35(2), 97–107.

[^bpmn]: [BPMN 2.0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BPMN) — Business Process Model and Notation, ISO/IEC 19510.

## One file, many views

| The same file is | Read by |
|:--|:--|
| A protocol | a colleague, a reviewer, an ethics board |
| An experiment | participants, or a model in the participant's seat |
| An analysis | the pipeline that ran, not a description of it |
| A figure | the Methods section of your paper |

The diagram is the source; every other [view](run/provenance.qmd) is a filtered reading of it, so they cannot fall out of step.
